body.p: In addition to the amendments discussed below, Claims 7, 9 and 19 have been amended to correct typographical errors. No new matter is believed to have been added by way of these amendments.
Accordingly, Claims 1-24 are currently pending for consideration. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration in view of the remarks set forth below.
A. Claim Interpretation under 35 U.S.C. & 112(f)

The Office Action alleges that the claims invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) because the claims allegedly recite a generic placeholder that is coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function and the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier.
Applicant does not concede to the Office's assertion that the claims invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) but acquiesces to the claims being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) for examination purposes.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully asserts that the claims no longer invoke an interpretation under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f). Reconsideration is respectfully requested.
B. Claim Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 4101

The following remarks are not to be used for claim construction or any other similar purpose, but are presented solely in connection with the § 101 analysis. Applicant further reserves the rights to make additional arguments.

The Office Action asserts that Claims 1-24 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 because the claims are allegedly directed to non-statutory subject matter. Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejection and disagrees that the claims are directed to an abstract idea without significantly more, and more specifically, a mental process, as alleged by the Office.
1. Legal Standard for Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 4 101
The Supreme Court has established a two-part test for subject matter eligibility. Part one of this eligibility analysis involves a determination as to whether the claims are "directed to" a

MPEP § 2106.04(d)(I) states that "Additional elements that represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity may integrate a recited judicial exception into a practical application." Limitations the courts have found indicative that an additional element (or combination of elements) may have integrated the exception into a practical application include: An improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to other technology or technical field, as discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a). See MPEP § 2106.04(d).

However, keeping all the past detecting results stored is

3. Step 2B - The claims recite additional elements that amount to significantly more
than the alleged judicial exception because the claims recite an improvement in the functioning of a computer AND an improvement to a technology or technical

The second part of the Alice/Mayo test is often referred to as a search for an inventive concept. Alice, 110 USPQ2d at 1976. MPEP § 2106.05 states that "Evaluating additional elements to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure that they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself."
MPEP § 2106.05(I)(A) provides examples of limitations that the courts have found to qualify as "significantly more" when recited in a claim with a judicial exception, such as:
a) Improvements to the functioning of a computer, e.g., a modification of
conventional Internet hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a dual- source hybrid webpage, as discussed in DDR Holdings;

modification of conventional rubber-molding processes to utilize a thermocouple inside the mold to constantly monitor the temperature and thus reduce under- and over-curing problems common in the art, as
discussed in Diamond. (Emphases added).

Applicant respectfully asserts that the additional elements provide an improvement in the functioning of a computer, and an improvement to other technology or technical field, that amount to significantly more than the alleged abstract idea.

As discussed above with respect to Step 2A (Prong Two), Applicant's Specification explicitly recites a technical problem that is solved by the technical solution that is provided by the features in Claim 1. Also, similar to the improved data compression in DDR Holdings, LLC, Applicant respectfully asserts that (i) the improvement in better management of the storage state of the result of detecting the object, (ii) the improvement in performing a high-performance travelling assistance operation, and (iii) the improvement in curbing an excessive increase in the processing load, which are provided by the features of Claim 1, demonstrate an improvement in computer-functionality that amounts to significantly more than the alleged judicial exception. Also, similar to the reduce under- and over-curing problems in Diamond, the several above- described improvements, which are provided by the features of Claim 1, demonstrate an improvement in the technical field of object detection performed by a vehicle that also amount to significantly more than the alleged judicial exception.

Therefore, for at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully asserts that the additional elements of Claim 1 amount to significantly more than the alleged abstract idea itself such that the claims are eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection is respectfully requested.
C. Claim Rejections under 35 U.S.C. & 103
Claims 1-24 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over JP 2009- 83647 A to Suzuki et al. (hereinafter "Suzuki") in view of U.S. 2018/0093663 to Kim et al. (hereinafter "Kim").
Application No. 17/404,535 Attorney Docket Number D2204.11159US01

The Patent and Trademark Office has the burden under 35 U.S.C. § 103 to establish aprima facie case of obviousness. The rationale to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious is that all the claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions, and the combination yielded nothing more than predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art. It can be important to identify a reason that would have prompted a person of ordinary skill in the relevant field to combine the elements in the way the claimed new subject matter does. If any of these findings cannot be made, then this rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art. MPEP § 2143.
2. Independent Claim 1
Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejection of Claim 1 but has amended the claim to expedite allowance. As amended, Claim 1 recites in part:
obtain a type of assistance operation that is currently being performed by the travelling assistance unit based on the related information;
determine storage priority of the object information in the object information storage unit based on the type of assistance operation; and
manage a storage state of the object information in the object information storage unit based on the storage priority.
The amendments are believed to be supported by at least 16, line 2 to page 17, line 9.
Applicant respectfully asserts that Suzuki and Kim, alone or in combination, fail to disclose at least the above feature(s) of amended Claim 1.

For example, Applicant respectfully asserts that the references fail to teach the feature(s) "obtain a type of assistance operation that is currently being performed by the travelling assistance unit based on the related information" and, further, to "determine storage priority of the object information in the object information storage unit based on the type of assistance operation".

In the rejection of Claim 1, the Office asserts that Suzuki teaches a storage priority of object information. However, in Suzuki, the order in which object information is stored is determined based on the time to collision (TTC) with the object. See Suzuki, page 4 ("In this case, it is preferable to store the object information with priority in the order of short collision time TTC.

Kim fails to remedy the deficiencies of Suzuki. The Office relies on Kim to an assistance operation of assisting travelling of the vehicle. However, Kim is silent in regard to the concept of storage priority and, even further, determining storage priority based on the type of assistance operation.
Therefore, for at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully asserts that Suzuki and Kim, alone or in combination, fail to disclose each and every feature of amended Claim 1.
Reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection is respectfully requested.
3. Independent Claim 13
Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejection of Claim 13 but has been amended the claim to expedite allowance. Claim 13 has been amended similarly as Claim 1.

Therefore, for at least the same reasons as asserted above with respect to amended Claim 1, Applicant respectfully asserts that Suzuki and Kim, alone or in combination, fail to disclose each and every feature of amended Claim 13. Reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection is respectfully requested.
4. Dependent Claims 2-12 and 14-24

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the rejections but submits that each of the dependent Claims 2-12 and 14-24 depends directly or indirectly on independent Claims 1 and 13. Thus, dependent Claims 2-12 and 14-24 incorporate by reference all the features of independent Claims 1 and 13. In view of the features as recited in the independent Claims 1 and 13, and in view of the additional features as recited in the dependent claims, Applicant respectfully submits that dependent Claims 2-12 and 14-24 are allowable for at least the reasons discussed above and their respective additional novel features. Although Applicant has not discussed specific features of all of the dependent claims in this response, Applicant does not necessarily agree with the characterizations and assessments made by the Examiner with respect to the dependent claims. Thus, Applicant respectfully submits that dependent Claims 2-12 and 14-24 are allowable.
